analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products like drugs, restricting advertising and youth access.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 38 House members including 4 Republicans, was sent to the House Commerce Committee in March 2000 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal drug law so the Food and Drug Administration could regulate tobacco products as drugs and devices. It would make the FDA's 1996 tobacco rule lawful, order stricter limits on marketing, advertising, and youth access, and require stronger warning labels modeled on the 1997 tobacco settlement proposal. It would also require states to adopt tobacco control programs or lose some federal tobacco-control funding. The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and a subcommittee, and it never came to a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially children and teens, gain because the bill gives the FDA power to restrict tobacco advertising and promotion, bar tobacco ads on broadcast media, require rotating health warnings, block unproven 'reduced risk' claims, and license retailers with inspections and penalties for selling to minors. State taxpayers also gain through model tobacco control programs backed by funding penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Declares the FDA's August 1996 tobacco regulation lawful and puts its remaining provisions into effect nine months after enactment, restoring federal controls on youth access and marketing that the FDA had issued but that lacked a clear statutory basis [S3].

Orders the Health and Human Services Secretary, within 18 months, to add the marketing, advertising, and access restrictions described in the 1997 tobacco settlement proposal, unless an advertising restriction would violate the First Amendment [S3].
Bans tobacco advertising on any electronic communication medium under FCC jurisdiction and requires new rotating warnings on cigarette and smokeless tobacco labels and ads [S3].

Bars manufacturers from claiming a tobacco product is reduced-risk unless the Secretary has determined it actually presents a significantly reduced health risk, and requires regulation of product ingredients [S3].

Requires states to enact model tobacco control programs, including retailer licensing, compliance inspections, performance goals, and penalties, or face withholding of up to 20 percent of federal tobacco control funds; the Secretary can also set up federal licensing in states that fail to implement [S3].

Repeals the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act and the Comprehensive Smokeless Tobacco Health Education Act once the new warning regulations take effect, replacing older labeling law with FDA authority [S3, S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the cost of stricter advertising limits, ingredient disclosure, new warnings, and reduced-risk claim restrictions, which shrink their marketing channels and could reduce sales. Tobacco retailers face licensing, inspection, and penalty requirements. Broadcast and print outlets that carry tobacco ads lose that revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco makers, retailers, and ad media

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the Secretary impose all the marketing and advertising restrictions from the 1997 settlement proposal, some of which were contested on First Amendment free-speech grounds, though it exempts any restriction that would violate the First Amendment [S3].

It preempts state and local governments from requiring any health statement on tobacco packages or ads other than the federally required warnings, which some state officials could see as limiting their own labeling rules [S3].

States face the loss of up to 20 percent of federal tobacco control funds if they fail to implement or achieve the performance goals of the model program, a mandate that shifts implementation burdens to state governments and retailers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For public health, the benefits are large: the bill restores federal authority to keep tobacco away from young people and curb marketing of the leading cause of preventable death, while including a First Amendment carve-out for advertising rules. The costs fall on the tobacco industry and, to a lesser degree, on retailers and states implementing licensing programs. The main design criticism is the federal preemption of extra state health statements, but on balance the bill is a public health measure whose costs are concentrated on the industry whose product drives the harm.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment subcommittee until Congress adjourned in January 2001, and never reached a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on March 21, 2000, joined by eight other House members, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce [S1, S3].
The bill attracted 38 cosponsors, 34 Democrats and 4 Republicans [S4].
On March 30, 2000, the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment, its last recorded action [S1].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in committee without a floor vote or Senate companion action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers are better off: they continued to market and sell without FDA jurisdiction over advertising, promotion, ingredients, or reduced-risk claims. Adults who would have faced stricter retail licensing and enforcement lost out as well.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the FDA Tobacco Jurisdiction Act of 2000 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 34 Democrats and 4 Republicans

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or a floor vote, leaving it pending in the Health and Environment subcommittee until Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (34 of 38) with token Republican support, and the Republican-controlled committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would subject tobacco products to FDA regulation, impose new warnings and advertising bans, require ingredient rules, and bar unproven reduced-risk claims, cutting into marketing freedom and likely sales. Its failure kept the industry outside FDA jurisdiction.

Retailers would face state or federal licensing, compliance inspections, and penalties including license suspension and revocation for selling to minors. These costs serve public health goals of restricting youth access.
The bill would bar tobacco advertising on FCC-regulated media and impose additional marketing restrictions under the FDA rule, removing a revenue stream from outlets that carry tobacco ads.
